title: Ranna Finds a Kannada Voice
subtitle: How Jain courts forged an epic tongue in stone and song
era: Age of Pampa, Ponna and Ranna, c. 941-993 CE
region: Karnataka courts from Vemulavada to Gangavadi
moral: A language grows when poets trust it with greatness.

sources.citation: Adipurana and Vikramarjuna Vijaya of Pampa, 941 CE; Shantipurana of Ponna; Ajitha Purana and Sahasa Bhima Vijaya of Ranna
sources.note: Primary Old Kannada literary corpus of the 10th century.

sources.citation: Attimabbe and Chavundaraya-related inscriptions honoring Ranna and Jain literary patronage
A.K. Ramanujan, Speaking of Siva introductory literary history; Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods; K.V. Ramesh on Kannada inscriptions
sources.note: Context for Kannada cosmopolitan and vernacular literary formation.

panels.shot: low-angle medium shot of a lone poet on a rocky hill, palm-leaf manuscript in hand, the great Gomaṭeśvara of Śravaṇabeḷagola rising behind him in twilight

dialogue.text: In an age when kings prayed in Sanskrit, Jain poets like Ranna dared to dream in Kannada, and turned a regional tongue into a language of heroes, renouncers and empire.

panels.shot: slow aerial sweep over the Deccan, from the Godavari plains to the hills of Karnataka, fading between temples, courts and Jain basadis

dialogue.text: Around the mid-tenth century, the Deccan hummed with dynasties and tongues—Rashtrakutas at Manyakheta, Vemulavada Chalukyas in the east, Western Gangas in Gangavadi—and Sanskrit still claimed the throne of high speech.

panels.shot: intimate interior wide shot of a Jain basadi library lit by oil lamps, palm-leaf bundles stacked high

dialogue.text: In the Jain basadis, however, another current gathered strength: monks copied Brahmi letters into Kannada scripts, students recited Prakrit gathas, and lay patrons listened as stories of Tirthankaras were retold in their own speech.

panels.shot: medium shot of a court scene in Vemulavada, with Pampa reciting before a seated king

dialogue.text: In 941, at Vemulavada, Pampa completed his Adipurana and Vikramarjuna Vijaya, proving that Kannada could carry both the cosmic spans of a Jina’s life and the martial glory of an Arjuna-like king.

panels.shot: courtly wide shot in a Rashtrakuta hall, with Ponna presenting a manuscript to a royal patron

dialogue.text: Ponna moved through Rashtrakuta circles, hailed in inscription and memory as a master of Shantipurana, blending ethical sermons with polished courtly Kannada for listeners who once expected only Sanskrit.

panels.shot: medium close-up of young Ranna in a modest Jain household, tracing letters on a tablet

dialogue.text: Into this world was born Ranna, a Jain layman of Karnataka, learning his first letters under the watchful gaze of both elders and images of the Jinas, hearing that Pampa and Ponna had already raised Kannada high.

panels.shot: wide shot of Shravanabelagola hill with pilgrims and scholars, Ranna in the crowd

dialogue.text: At Shravanabelagola, the Western Ganga stronghold of Jain piety, stone hills, basadis and the colossal Bahubali drew scholars and patrons together, and Ranna’s steps joined this flow of devotion and learning.

panels.shot: interior medium shot in a Ganga noble’s hall, Chavundaraya listening as Ranna recites

dialogue.text: Inscription and tradition remember Ranna among those linked to Chavundaraya, the great Ganga general and patron, whose own commissioning of Jain works created the very circles in which Kannada letters could thrive.

panels.shot: close-up on Ranna’s face, torn between two manuscripts—one Sanskrit, one Kannada

dialogue.speaker: Ranna, Jewel of the Jain Poets
dialogue.text: Can our own tongue bear the weight of Bhima’s courage and the Jinas’ truth?

panels.shot: medium shot of Ranna composing, with an image of Ajitha or a Tirthankara before him

dialogue.text: Ranna’s first known work, Ajitha Purana, retold the life of the second Tirthankara, Ajitanatha, in Kannada, bringing a Jina’s calm renunciation into the earthy rhythm of a tongue spoken in markets and courts.

panels.shot: dynamic low-angle shot of Ranna narrating a battle scene from Sahasa Bhima Vijaya to an attentive mixed audience

dialogue.text: With Sahasa Bhima Vijaya, also known as Gadayuddha, Ranna cast the Mahabharata’s mace-duel into Kannada, yet under Jain patronage he shaped Bhima’s courage within a frame that still remembered restraint and karma.

panels.shot: medium shot in a later Chalukya court, king Satyashraya honoring Ranna before assembled nobles

dialogue.text: Ranna’s fame spread; under the later Chalukyas he was honored as a jewel among poets, proof that a writer shaped in Jain-Ganga circles could now stand at the heart of a royal Kannada cosmopolis.

panels.shot: quiet wide shot of Ranna and his patron Attimabbe overseeing the copying of manuscripts

dialogue.text: Later inscriptions praise Attimabbe for having hundreds of Kannada copies of Jain texts made and gifted, showing how women patrons and scribes carried Ranna’s words far beyond the courts that first heard them.

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot blending three scenes: Pampa at Vemulavada, Ponna at Manyakheta, Ranna in Karnataka, all linked by flowing Kannada script

dialogue.text: The three gems—Pampa in Vemulavada, Ponna in Rashtrakuta halls, Ranna in Jain-Ganga and Chalukya circles—did not sit together at one Ganga court, yet their works shared a network of faith, patronage and language.

panels.shot: close-up of a stone inscription mentioning Ranna and Jain patrons, with Ranna’s faint reflection on the polished stone

dialogue.text: Epigraphs carved in stone remember these ties: gifts of land to basadis, praise for poets, the naming of works—evidence that Kannada’s literary rise was anchored not only in imagination but in endowments and institutions.

panels.shot: wide shot of a present-day library table with old palm-leaf manuscripts of Pampa, Ponna and Ranna laid out together

dialogue.text: Today, when scholars open the palm leaves of Adipurana, Shantipurana and Sahasa Bhima Vijaya, they see how a Jain literary ecology, sustained by Ganga and other courts, slowly shifted Kannada from margin to epic center.

panels.shot: final contemplative medium shot of Ranna looking out over the Kannada countryside, manuscript closed in his hands

dialogue.text: Ranna’s journey shows that a language grows when poets trust it with greatness, and that when faith, power and art meet in living tongues, they leave echoes louder than any empire’s stone.
